record.original_question: Is a flexibly permutation-stable group always permutation-stable?

evidence.quote: Is a flexibly permutation-stable group always permutation-stable?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with a fixed finite generating set $S$, and let $F_S$ denote the free group on $S$. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\mathrm{Sym}(N)$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,\dots,N\}$, equipped with the normalized Hamming distance $d_H(\sigma,\tau) = \frac{1}{N}|\{i : \sigma(i)\neq \tau(i)\}|$. For $M \geq N$, regard $\mathrm{Sym}(N)$ as a subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(M)$ by fixing the points $N+1,\dots,M$.

A homomorphism $\varphi : F_S \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ is called an $\varepsilon$-almost action of $G$ if for every relation $r$ in $G$ (i.e., every $r$ in the kernel of the canonical map $F_S \to G$ from some, equivalently any, presentation), $d_H(\varphi(r), \mathrm{id}) \leq \varepsilon$. (For finitely presented $G$ it suffices to require this for the finitely many defining relations.)

The group $G$ is called permutation-stable (P-stable) if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that whenever $\varphi : F_S \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ is a $\delta$-almost action, there is an honest homomorphism $\psi : G \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ (i.e., a homomorphism $F_S \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ that factors through $G$) with $\max_{s \in S} d_H(\varphi(s), \psi(s)) \leq \varepsilon$.

The group $G$ is called flexibly permutation-stable if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that whenever $\varphi : F_S \to \mathrm{Sym}(N)$ is a $\delta$-almost action, there exist $M \geq N$ and an honest homomorphism $\psi : G \to \mathrm{Sym}(M)$ with
$$\max_{s \in S} \frac{1}{M}\big|\{i \in \{1,\dots,M\} : \varphi(s)(i) \neq \psi(s)(i)\}\big| \leq \varepsilon,$$
where $\varphi(s)$ is viewed in $\mathrm{Sym}(M)$ via the natural embedding above.

Both properties are independent of the choice of finite generating set $S$ (and of presentation) and are thus invariants of the group $G$.

Question: Must every flexibly permutation-stable group be permutation-stable?
artifact.status_search_result: The relationship between flexible permutation-stability and (strict) permutation-stability is an active research topic. Surface groups have been shown to be flexibly stable, but no separation between the two notions is known, and the implication "flexibly P-stable implies P-stable" is generally listed as an open problem in the area.

status_evidence.title: Surface groups are flexibly stable
status_evidence.snippet: Surface groups are flexibly stable in permutations; flexible stability is a relaxed version of permutation stability and the methods used towards proving flexible stability will in general increase the total area, so flexible rather than strict stability is established.
status_evidence.claim: Flexible permutation-stability is known to be a strictly more accessible property to establish than strict permutation-stability, and whether the two notions coincide for groups remains a recognized open question.

status_evidence.title: Stability for product groups and property (τ)
status_evidence.snippet: Some groups are not even flexibly P-stable, giving the first non-amenable residually finite examples; F_m × Z^d and F_m × F_n are not P-stable.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work distinguishes failures of flexible P-stability from failures of P-stability but does not resolve whether flexibly P-stable implies P-stable.
